# March — Progress Summary

## What Is March

A statically-typed functional programming language. The compiler is implemented in OCaml 5.3.0. The name is "March."

## Design Decisions Made

### Type System
- **Hindley-Milner inference with bidirectional type checking** at function boundaries — balances inference convenience with good error localization
- **Type annotations optional** everywhere except where inference fails (recursive functions, ambiguous overloads)
- **Linear and affine types** for ownership, safe mutation, actor message-passing isolation, and FFI safety
- **Provenance-tracking types** — every type constraint carries a *reason* chain (not just a span), so errors explain *why* a type was expected
- **Error recovery via typed hole injection** — errors become typed holes; the compiler continues and reports multiple diagnostics. Same mechanism as user-written `?` holes.
- **Unboxed types / representation polymorphism** — compiler chooses boxed vs unboxed based on usage, after monomorphization
- **Type-level naturals** — `Nat` in type parameters with `+`, `*`, equality. Enables `Vector(n, a)`, `Matrix(m, n, a)`, `NDArray(shape, a)` with compile-time dimension checking. Not full dependent types.
- **Refinement-types Z3 bridge (Phase A0)** — `lib/refine/`: SMT-LIB2 renderer for the Int/Bool linear-arithmetic + EUF fragment (`Smt`), a `(get-model)` s-expression parser (`Model`), a long-lived `z3 -in` driver with push/pop per VC (`Solver`), a BLAKE3-keyed verdict cache under `.march/cas/vc/` (`Vc_cache`), and a cache→solver→outcome orchestrator (`Refine.discharge`). Standalone and unit-tested (`test/test_refine.ml`, 14 cases); solver tests skip gracefully when z3 is absent. Not yet wired into the typechecker (that is Phase A1). Spec: `specs/2026-06-20-dependent-types-refinements-design.md`; plan: `specs/plans/2026-06-20-refinement-types-a0-z3-bridge.md`.
- **Refinement-types surface syntax + erasure (Phase A1a)** — `{T | predicate}` and `{v : T | predicate}` parse to a new `Ast.TyRefine` node (moved into `expr`'s recursive group so the predicate is an `expr`; `_` is now an expression atom for the refinement-value placeholder). Every exhaustive `Ast.ty` match erases the refinement to its base type, so the full pipeline accepts refined annotations and typechecks them identically to the base — **no checking yet** (VC emission is A1b). Formatter renders the predicate faithfully via a forward-ref to the expr printer. 3 parser tests. Plan: `specs/plans/2026-06-21-refinement-types-a1-typechecker-wiring.md`.
- **Refinement-types Tier 0 postcondition propagation** — a function's declared return refinement (a *closed* postcondition, i.e. one that doesn't mention a parameter) is recorded in `fn_sig.ret` and consumed at call sites, so `takepos(neg())` and `let c = neg() ... takepos(c)` are both compile errors when `neg`'s `{Int | _ < 0}` return is disjoint from `takepos`'s `{Int | _ >= 0}` parameter. Resolution mirrors ordinary call resolution — direct named calls, across modules, through `alias`/`use`. A *relational* postcondition (one mentioning a parameter, e.g. `{Int | _ < n}`) is checked at the definition but deliberately NOT propagated — instantiating it at a call site needs substituting arguments for parameters, which is future (Tier 1) work. **Only POSITIVELY VERIFIED postconditions propagate**: the definition-side check still rejects only a postcondition that can *never* hold (so an unprovable-but-correct one stays legal), but a postcondition that was not proven on every return path of every clause is cleared from `fn_sig.ret` before the walk and tells callers nothing. Propagated facts are *added* to the assumptions a call-site VC discharges against, so trusting an unproven contract would make violations easier to "prove" — i.e. it would be a false-positive engine, which this subsystem's no-false-positives stance forbids.
- **No algebraic effects** (removed — concurrency is actors + message passing)
- **ADTs use capitalized constructors** (`Ok`, `Err`, `Some`, `None`) — atoms (`:name`) are lightweight runtime tags for messaging, not type constructors
- **Pony-style capabilities**: No. Linear/affine is the ceiling.

### Module System
- **`mod Name do ... end`** — namespaces; definitions private by default, `pub` to export
- **`sig Name do ... end`** — explicit interface declarations; get their own hash separate from implementation hashes. Downstream code depends on the sig hash — internal refactors don't invalidate downstream caches.
- **`interface Name(a) do ... end`** — typeclasses with default implementations and associated types; covers ML functor use cases without functor complexity
- **`impl Interface(Type) do ... end`** — implement an interface for a type, with conditional impls via `when` constraints
- **Content-addressed versioning** — names are aliases to hashes; the build system auto-generates a lockfile of resolved hashes. No version numbers. No dependency conflicts (different hashes coexist).

### Built-in Types
- **Primitives**: `Int` (64-bit), `Float` (64-bit), `Byte` (8-bit), `Bool`, `String` (UTF-8), `Char` (Unicode scalar)
- **Stdlib numeric**: `BigInt`, `Decimal` (exact, for money/finance), `Ratio` — numeric abstraction via `Num`/`Fractional` interfaces
- **Strings**: `String`, `Char`, `Rope` (stdlib), `Regex` (stdlib). String interpolation via `${}` desugared to `Interpolatable` interface.
- **Collections**: `List(a)`, `Array(a)` (fixed-size contiguous), `Map(k, v)`, `Set(a)`, `Option(a)`, `Result(a, e)`
- **Sized arrays**: `Vector(n, a)`, `Matrix(m, n, a)`, `NDArray(shape, a)` — dimension-checked at compile time via type-level naturals
- **Concurrency**: `Pid(a)`, `Cap(a)`, `Future(a)`, `Stream(a)`, `Task(a)` (structured concurrency), `Node`
- **Constraints**: `Sendable(a)` — compiler-derived, marks types safe to cross node/thread boundaries
- **FFI**: `linear Ptr(a)`, per-library `Cap(LibName)`

### Concurrency
- **Actors** — share-nothing message passing with private state, isolation guaranteed by linear types
- **Actor state updates** use record spread: `{ state with field = new_value }`
- **Binary session types** for v1 — typed two-party protocols verified at compile time (catches deadlocks, protocol violations, missing cases). Multi-party deferred post-v1.
- **Capability-secure messaging** — actors can only message actors they hold an unforgeable capability reference to; linear capabilities enable ownership transfer
- **Content-addressed message schemas** — messages reference their schema by hash for safe distributed communication
- **Location-transparent `Pid`** (Erlang model) — you don't know or care which node an actor lives on
- **`Future(a)`** for async actor results, **`Stream(a)`** for ongoing sequences, **`Task(a)`** for structured parallel compute

### Syntax (ML/Elixir Hybrid)
- `fn name(x, y) do ... end` — named functions with parenthesized args
- `fn x -> x + 1` / `fn (x, y) -> body` — lambdas; multi-param requires parens; lambda bodies support leading `let` bindings + final expr (same as match arm block bodies). As an inline call argument (`f(fn x -> ...)`), the body additionally accepts bare (non-`let`) statements before the final expression, since the argument is unambiguously bounded by `,`/`)`; a `let`-bound lambda used elsewhere (e.g. as a `let` RHS) stays restricted to `let`*-then-final-expr, since there's no such boundary there.
- `mod Name do ... end` — modules; `sig Name do ... end` — interfaces
- `do ... end` — inline block expression (also valid in match arms)
- `x |> f |> g` — pipe operator
- `let x = expr` — block-scoped, no `in` keyword; subsequent exprs in the block see the binding
- `match expr with | Pat -> body end` — pattern matching; arm bodies are `block_body` (multi-expr ok)
- `if cond then e1 else e2` — conditional expression
- `?name` / `?` — typed holes
- `:ok`, `:error` — atoms as typed tags belonging to declared atom sets
- **Function head matching** — consecutive `fn` clauses with the same name are grouped (Elixir-style multi-head)
- `when` guards on function heads and match branches
- `--` line comments, `{- -}` nested block comments
- Type variants: `type Foo = A | B(Int)` — no leading `|`

### Compiler Backend
- **Whole-program monomorphization** — all polymorphic functions specialized to concrete types (like Rust/MLton)
- **Defunctionalization** — closures become tagged unions + dispatch (no closure allocation, no indirect calls)
- **Content-addressed code** — whole-definition hashing (SHA-256), names are aliases to hashes
- **Query-based/demand-driven compiler architecture** (not a pipeline) — incremental recompilation falls out naturally
- **Compilation target**: LLVM IR

### Compiler Pass Order
1. Parse (with hole injection on error)
2. Desugar multi-head functions → single function with match (Erlang-style)
3. Type check (bidirectional, provenance-tracked, linearity)
4. Session type verification (on actor/protocol code)
5. Strip provenance metadata
6. Monomorphize (resolve representation polymorphism)
7. Defunctionalize (closures → tagged unions)
8. Code generation

## Implementation Language
- **OCaml 5.3.0** via opam switch named `march`
- Dependencies: dune, menhir, ppx_deriving, alcotest, odoc
- `opam` and `dune` are available directly in PATH (source `~/.zshrc` first if needed)

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement postconditions: a named return binder no longer captures body variables in the path context)

**A live false positive, reproduced against the built compiler before the fix.** `fn f(v : Int, k : Int) : {v : Int | v > 0} do if v < 0 do k else 1 end end` was reported as "does not satisfy its return type constraint" with the counterexample `k = -1`. The guard `v < 0` is about the PARAMETER `v`; `check_post` translated the path conditions with the SAME `resolve_var` as the return predicate, in which the binder `v` denotes the RETURN value, so the guard became `k < 0` and made `v > 0` (i.e. `k > 0`) definitely false.

This is the same caller/callee conflation already fixed for `check_call`'s path conditions (`path_resolve_var`), reaching the postcondition side by the same route: a path condition is collected from the function BODY, so every name in it is a body name and denotes itself, while the return binder is not a body name at all — it exists only inside the refinement predicate.

**The bug cut both ways.** With the tail `0` instead of `k`, the same collision turned `v < 0` into `0 < 0`: a contradictory assumption, under which the goal discharges vacuously and a GENUINE violation went unreported. That shape is pinned as a second test and was silent before the fix.

Path conditions now go through a `path_resolve_var` / `path_resolve_field` pair resolving through the enclosing scope (`var_const` and `scope_field_resolver`). `_` is deliberately left pointing at the return term: it is not a legal variable in body code, so it can only have come from a predicate, and routing it through `var_const` would declare a constant named `_`. Four tests in `post_suite` — the false positive, the suppressed-violation control, a control that a non-colliding named binder still denotes the return value in the PREDICATE, and one that a guard on the colliding parameter still discharges when the tail IS that parameter (the case the binder reading got right only by accident).

Practical exposure was low — return binders are almost always `_` — but it was a live misattribution path, and a false positive is this subsystem's cardinal sin.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement types: an unreflectable record field no longer sinks its siblings)

**`serve({ port: 9, history: Cons(1, Nil) })` was skipped whole.** `term_fits_sort` rejects `Cons(1, Nil)`: the built-in `List` is generic, so its element field carries the opaque sort `Elem` and the scalar reflection's integer `1` cannot sit there. `reflect_record_literal` then returned `None` for the ENTIRE record, so the perfectly checkable `port` field was lost along with the one field nobody could see. The same happened for `{ port: 0, name: n }` with a `String`-typed `n`.

**Fix: an opaque stand-in, not a coerced term.** `reflect_record_literal` gained an OPTIONAL `~opaque` that mints a fresh constant at the offending field's DECLARED sort. The ill-sorted `(Cons 1 Nil)` is still never built — the channel-poisoning hazard the original skip existed to prevent (a malformed VC makes z3 emit an `(error …)` that desynchronises the shared `z3 -in` channel and silently disables refinement checking for the rest of the compilation) is untouched. This is deliberately NOT the "make `Int` fit `Elem`" route.

**Soundness.** The stand-in carries no assumptions, so it denotes an arbitrary value of its sort. The call-site decision procedure reports only when `¬goal` is VERIFIED — valid under EVERY assignment — so a goal that depends on the stand-in is never reported *and* never discharged, while a goal that depends only on the reflected siblings is decided exactly as if the record were fully known. Pinned in both directions: a predicate about the opaque field stays silent whether its real value satisfies it (`{count: 1, history: Cons(1, Nil)}` against `len(v.history) == v.count`) or violates it (`count: 5`).

**Call-site only, on purpose.** `check_post` switches to "a SAT model over a concrete record in scope is a definite violation"; a model free to assign the stand-in a bad value would be reported as a counterexample although the real field holds a fine value — a false positive. The return side therefore never passes `~opaque`, and a test pins that it still skips the whole record.

Two existing tests flipped from asserting silence to asserting an error (`{ port: 0, name: n }` and `{ port: 0, history: Cons(1, Nil) }` against `{v : Config | v.port >= 1}`). Both are genuine violations that were being lost to a sibling field, and both test comments were rewritten to state why the channel-safety rationale still holds.

Feature list addition:

- A record argument with an **unreflectable field** (a `String` bound to a variable, a list literal with concrete elements) is still checked on its reflectable fields at a call site; only the unreflectable field is opaque.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement types: record FIELD facts flow into path conditions)

**A guard on a record field now reaches the call it guards.** `if c.port >= 1 do serve(c)` discharges a `{v : Config | v.port >= 1}` precondition, and the contradictory `if c.port <= 0 do serve(c)` is reported as a definite failure. The condition was already being collected into the `path` context — it was dropped at translation time, because the path translation in `check_call` passed no `~resolve_field` to `smt_of`, so `c.port` reflected to `None` and the whole condition went away. (`make_field_resolver` already existed; only `check_post` consulted it.)

**Two halves were missing, and each is useless without the other.** (1) A new `recenv` — `name -> SMT sort` for variables whose DECLARED type is a registered record, refined or not — because `scope` carries only *refined* locals and a plain `c : Config` parameter was invisible to it. Populated from fn/lambda parameters, annotated `let`s, an unannotated `let c = d` aliasing a known record, and a bare `PatVar` `match` binder on a record-typed variable scrutinee (each denotes the same value as its source, so sharing one SMT constant is correct). It carries no predicate: an entry is a wholly unconstrained datatype constant, so on its own it proves nothing in either direction — an entry can only turn a *skip* into a check the guards actually decide, never into a guess. (2) `check_call`'s `record_self` now also reflects an UNREFINED record variable to that same constant. Previously it required a `scope` entry and returned `None` otherwise, which set `mode = \`Skip\`` and built no goal at all — so a guarded call could never discharge, *and* a guard that made the call a definite failure was never reported.

**The delicate part was sort collisions, not the fact plumbing.** A record name is declared into its datatype sort by the new `path_resolve_field`, so every other producer must refuse to declare it `Int`: `path_resolve_var` and `resolve_var`'s caller-scope fallback both now return `None` for such a name. One symbol declared at two sorts makes z3 answer with an `(error …)`, and that error desynchronises the long-lived `z3 -in` channel — silently disabling refinement checking for the remainder of the compilation, which is the worst failure this subsystem has (its symptom is silence). A dedicated co-occurrence test asserts a record field guard and an unrelated Int violation in one module still yield exactly one reported violation.

**Shadow discipline was verified by negative control, not by assertion.** The path context is the channel that produced false positives in the ADT round, and this adds a new fact source to it. New `record-path-facts` group in `test/test_refinecheck.ml` (11 tests). With `path_shadow` stubbed to the identity, the `let`, lambda-parameter and `match`-binder cases all FAIL — they report a violation on correct code — and pass again with it restored, so those three are genuine false-positive detectors rather than tests that would pass either way. The `let?` case is honestly non-discriminating and is labelled as such in the test source: a `let?` binder can carry no type annotation (`let? x : T = …` is a dedicated parse error) and March has no annotated-expression form, so the payload's record type is never visible to `recenv`; the inner call is skipped for that unrelated reason and the case would stay silent whatever `ELetQ` did. `recenv_shadow` is defense-in-depth rather than load-bearing — stubbing it alone changes no verdict, since `path_shadow` drops any condition *mentioning* the name, a strict superset — but it is kept because the identity channel is what would bite if a fact ever reached the callee by another route.

Feature list addition:

- Refinement checking uses **record field guards** as path facts: `if c.port >= 1 do serve(c)` discharges a record precondition on a plainly-typed `c : Config`, and a contradictory guard is reported.
## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, Tier 1 relational postconditions — a return refinement mentioning a parameter now propagates to call sites)

**`pred_is_closed` became `classify_pred`; `postcond_of` instantiates.** Tier 0 recorded a callee's *closed* return refinement in `fn_sig.ret` and consumed it at call sites, but `pred_is_closed` rejected any predicate mentioning a parameter, so `fn below(n : Int) : {Int | _ < n}` told callers nothing. The filter lived in exactly one place by design (`postcond_of`, consulted by both propagation sites), so this was a bounded change to a 2900-line file. `classify_pred : string -> string list -> A.expr -> pred_scope` now returns `Closed` (mentions only the binder — Tier 0, returned unchanged), `Relational of string list` (mentions the binder plus these parameters), or `Unusable` (mentions anything else, or syntax the checker cannot reflect — the conservative `_ -> bad := true` catch-all is retained verbatim from `pred_is_closed`). `postcond_of` gained the call's actual arguments and returns a predicate already restated in the **caller's** namespace, so `scope_add_binding` (a `let` bound to a call) and `reflect_scalar` (an inline call argument) needed only to thread `args` through — no substitution logic of their own, and the existing scope/reflection machinery is untouched.

**Substitution, not resolution — and simultaneous.** The `let` site stores the predicate in `scope` for use at a *later* call, by which point the actuals are out of reach, so a captured resolver would have to be carried along; rewriting the predicate AST instead produces something the existing machinery already handles. `subst_params` applies the whole formal→actual map in ONE traversal: with `fn f(n : Int, m : Int) : {Int | _ < n + m}` called as `f(m, 1)`, a sequential rewrite (`n := m`, then `m := 1`) would rewrite the freshly-introduced `m` and manufacture `_ < 1 + 1` — a fact about the caller that was never proven. An application's **head** is deliberately never substituted (guarded explicitly with a dedicated `A.EApp ((A.EVar _ as hd), …)` arm): it names a function, operator or measure, not a value, so a formal named `len` cannot turn `len(xs)` into `40(xs)`. Formals map to actuals **positionally**, matching the convention the precondition side's `check_call`/`actual_of_name` has always used.

**Skip, don't guess.** If any parameter the predicate mentions has no corresponding actual (arity mismatch, an omitted defaulted argument), the entire instantiation is abandoned and nothing propagates. A *partially* substituted predicate would mix the callee's and the caller's namespaces — precisely the conflation behind an earlier false-positive class in this subsystem. A formal recorded as `"_"` (a pattern parameter, via `sig_of_clause`) is likewise excluded from the map, since `"_"` is also the refinement binder's own spelling and mapping it would rewrite the binder itself.

**The Tier 0 safety guarantee is inherited, not rebuilt.** `gate_unverified_posts` already clears `ret` on every signature whose postcondition the definition side did not POSITIVELY VERIFY, and relational postconditions pass through the same gate. Confirmed by temporary instrumentation rather than assumed: `below`'s `_ < n` reports `verified=true`, while `shady`'s (`_ < n` over a body the solver cannot analyse) reports `verified=false` and its contract is cleared — so a stale or unprovable relational contract cannot flag correct code. **Known conservatism found while probing:** desugar rewrites EVERY parameter of a clause containing a pattern parameter to `__arg0`/`__arg1`, so such a callee's predicate no longer mentions any recognised formal, classifies `Unusable`, and simply does not propagate. Silence, the safe direction. (This also means the undesugared unit-test entry point `has_refine_error` and the desugared production path reach the same outcome by two different routes — the `"_"` exclusion covers the former, `Unusable` the latter.)

One pre-existing test changed meaning rather than being added to: `tier0_suite`'s "relational postcondition is NOT propagated (Tier 1 boundary)" asserted SILENCE for `let c = below(0); takepos(c)` and was the explicit marker for the boundary this work removes; it now asserts the violation is reported and is renamed accordingly.

13-program adversarial sweep, each run on a cold `.march/cas/vc`: a caller variable sharing a callee formal's name (and refined `<= 0`, so a conflation WOULD flag it), a pattern formal, a satisfiable literal instantiation, instantiation inside a `match` arm and both `if` branches, a `let`-bound relational result shadowed four ways (inner `let`, lambda parameter, `let?`, `match` binder), a `len`-of-list-parameter predicate, a formal sharing the measure name `len`, a call with more arguments than the predicate mentions, and a recursive relational postcondition — **all exit 0**. The headline `takepos(below(0))` exits 1. Two negative controls confirm the sweep is not vacuous: moving the violating value into the third argument position makes the positional case exit 1. A six-kind multi-violation file (relational, record field, String, ADT tag, list bounds, plain Int) reports all six with zero `(error` in the output, so no VC desynced the shared z3 channel. `test_refinecheck.exe`: 154 tests, exit 0 (was 137); `test_refine`, `run_compiler` (556), `run_eval` (250) all exit 0.

Feature list addition:

- Relational postconditions propagate to call sites. A return refinement mentioning a parameter (`fn below(n : Int) : {Int | _ < n}`) is instantiated at each call by substituting that call's arguments, so `takepos(below(0))` is a compile error while `takepos(below(10))` is silent. Substitution is simultaneous and positional, application heads (measures/operators) are never rewritten, and instantiation is skipped wholesale rather than done partially — as before, only postconditions the definition side actually proved travel at all.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, or-patterns (`p1 | p2 | p3`) added — the only pattern-matcher gap needing a new AST constructor)

**`Ast.pattern` gains `PatOr of pattern list * span`.** Task 5 (final) of `specs/plans/2026-07-24-pattern-matching-gaps.md`. Unlike the previous four tasks in this plan, which each wired up an AST constructor that already existed, or-patterns did not exist anywhere in the AST before this task — so the change ripples through every exhaustive `match` over `Ast.pattern` in the codebase. Grammar: `pattern_no_as` gains an or layer beneath the existing `as`-alias layer (`pattern: pattern_no_as AS lower_name`, Task 2), with `pattern_no_as`'s former alternatives (constructor/atom/`simple_pattern`) renamed down to a new `pattern_alt`: `pattern_no_as: pattern_alt PIPE separated_nonempty_list(PIPE, pattern_alt) | pattern_alt`. `PIPE` already serves as `arm_sep` (`NL | PIPE` between match arms), but an arm separator only ever follows a COMPLETE branch (one that has already consumed its `ARROW` and body), so LR(1) distinguishes the two uses with no conflict — verified empirically before writing the production (baseline 9 shift/reduce conflicts) and reconfirmed after (still 9, `menhir --explain`). Adding the constructor forced the OCaml compiler (warning-8-as-error) to enumerate every non-exhaustive match: `lib/typecheck/typecheck.ml` (`infer_pattern`, `norm_pat`, `span_of_pat`, `collect_pattern_vars`, `free_vars_pattern`, `pat_has_record`, the ctor-owner walker), `lib/eval/eval.ml` (`match_pattern`), `lib/tir/lower_match.ml` (`span_of_pat`, `collect_pat_names`, `pat_tag_and_subs`), and one mechanical arm each in `lib/ast/span_remap.ml`, `lib/desugar/desugar.ml` (three sites: `pat_binds_conn`, `respan_pat`, `add_pat_vars`), `lib/dump/ast_json.ml`, `lib/format/format.ml`, `lib/refactor/refactor.ml`, `lib/refinecheck/refine_check.ml`, `lsp/lib/workspace.ml`, and `lsp/lib/analysis.ml` (two sites; several OTHER `analysis.ml` pattern-walkers already had a pre-existing `_ ->` catch-all and needed no change, since a valid or-pattern binds nothing they could ever observe there).

**Scope, by design: alternatives that bind no variables** (`1 | 2 | 3`, `:get | :head`, `Red | Blue`). An alternative that binds a variable (`A(x) | B(x) -> x`) is rejected at typecheck with a dedicated diagnostic (`` Or-pattern alternatives cannot bind variables (`x`). ``, code `or_pattern_binding`) — not a stopgap, a hard restriction with a structural reason: every alternative shares ONE arm body via `lower_match.ml`'s existing 0-arg join point (`hoist_fallback_jp`), which has nowhere to put a per-alternative binding — `A(x)`'s `x` and `B(x)`'s `x` would need to be bound to DIFFERENT values depending on which alternative actually matched, but the shared call site takes no arguments. Lifting this needs n-ary join points (hoist the body as a function of the bound variables, have each split row call it with its own bindings) — filed as a follow-up in `specs/todos.md`, not attempted here. The workaround of duplicating the arm body once per alternative was explicitly rejected too: it reintroduces exactly the exponential TIR blowup `hoist_fallback_jp` exists to prevent.

Interpreter: `match_pattern`'s new `PatOr` case tries each alternative in order, first match wins (`§4.3`). Exhaustiveness/redundancy: `norm_pat` maps `PatOr` to `SPWild` (conservative — same treatment `PatRecord` already gets), but a new `norm_pat_rows` wrapper expands a pattern into the `spat` row(s) it covers — one per alternative for an or-pattern, one for everything else — and both `check_exhaustiveness`'s guardless/full matrices and `check_redundant_arms`'s prefix now flat-map through it. Consequence: `Red | Green` plus a `Blue` arm is correctly seen as exhaustive for a three-constructor `Color` (dropping `Blue` still warns), and `check_redundant_arms` flags an arm redundant only if **every** alternative is already subsumed by the prefix (`List.exists ... is_useful` over the expanded rows, not "any"), so a partially-live or-pattern arm is never falsely flagged.

Lowering (`lib/tir/lower_match.ml`): new `expand_or_rows`, next to `strip_as_column` — splits a row whose first column is a `PatOr` into one row per alternative, all sharing the same body expression; `pat_tag_and_subs` returns `None` for `PatOr` (split before tag dispatch is ever reached, so it never sees one — same disposition as `PatRecord`). Splitting the row means the shared body value now sits at N leaf positions in the eventual decision tree; without care that duplicates the body's emitted code N times when the tree is walked to LLVM IR. Both of `lower_match`'s paths (the no-guard fast path AND the per-branch guarded path) now check `pat_has_or` on each arm's pattern and, when true, hoist the arm body into a shared 0-arg join point via `hoist_fallback_jp` BEFORE the row ever reaches `expand_or_rows` — every split alternative then references the cheap `EApp(clo_var, [])` call instead of a full copy of the body, exactly mirroring the existing fallback-hoisting discipline `hoist_fallback_jp` was built for.

New `or_patterns` group in `test/test_eval.ml` (2 tests: literal alternatives via `1 | 2 | 3`, nullary-constructor alternatives via `Red | Green`) plus `test_or_pattern_binding_rejected` / `test_or_pattern_nonbinding_accepted` / `test_or_pattern_exhaustiveness` in `test/test_compiler.ml`'s `match_diagnostics` group, plus a compiled round-trip (`test/native/or_pattern.march`, diffed against `.expected` — `size(1)`/`size(3)`/`size(9)` and `warm(Red)`/`warm(Blue)`). Grammar conformance corpus: `parse/p32_or_pattern.march` added (well-typed, `--check` exit 0) — corpus is 32 parse + 12 reject = 44 total, `grammar-check` green. The binding-rejection witness is a **type** error, not a parse error (`A(x) | B(x)` parses fine and only fails to typecheck), so it belongs in the types corpus instead of grammar/reject: `specs/lang/types/reject/t82_or_pattern_binding.march` — types corpus is 90 accept + 82 reject = 172 total, `types-check` green. Docs updated in the same commit: `specs/lang/grammar.md` (new §6.4 for `PatOr`, and the §6.2 EBNF rewritten to show the full `pattern`/`pattern_no_as`/`pattern_alt` three-layer hierarchy plus the `PIPE` dual-use finding), `specs/lang/core-march-types.md` (new `(P-Or)` typing rule alongside `(P-Record)`/`(P-As)`), `specs/lang/pattern-matching.md` + `docs/pattern-matching.md` (new "Or Patterns" section — syntax, first-match-wins semantics, the no-bindings restriction and its two workarounds), `specs/lang/surface-syntax.md` + `.claude/skills/march-lang/SKILL.md` (quick-reference examples), `CHANGELOG.md`. `scripts/check-docs.sh` green (all three conformance-corpus count sites — golden/types/grammar — verified consistent). Full suite: `run_eval` 250/250, `run_compiler` 551/551, `run_snapshots` 31/31 (byte-identical — or-patterns don't appear in the TIR snapshot corpus, so no churn), `run_codegen` 444/444, `run_stdlib` 815/816 (the one non-pass is the same pre-existing, machine-wide ASAN 30s livelock in `MARCH_SANITIZE` teardown, independently verified: a trivial unrelated `clang -fsanitize=address` hello-world hangs identically on this host under the same load).

Feature list addition:

- Or-patterns (`p1 | p2 | p3`) in `match` arms — matches an arm against several alternatives (literals, nullary/atom constructors, or any other non-binding pattern shape), trying each in order and running the shared arm body on the first that matches. Alternatives may not bind variables (`A(x) | B(x)` is a dedicated typecheck error, `or_pattern_binding`) — split into separate arms, or match the common shape and test the difference with a `when` guard.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, record patterns gained open field lists — `{ x }` now matches any record with an `x` field)

**`PatRecord` field lists are open in a `match` arm** (and, transitively, in a function parameter that dispatches through one), not just full destructures. Task 4 of `specs/plans/2026-07-24-pattern-matching-gaps.md`. Task 3 (entry below) made `PatRecord` reachable from surface syntax but only for a field list that EXACTLY matched the scrutinee's own fields: `infer_pattern`'s `PatRecord` arm synthesized a CLOSED `TRecord` from just the mentioned fields, and `unify` (`typecheck.ml:2789`) requires exact field-set equality (no width subtyping, no row variables in March's record system), so `{ x }` against `{ x: Int, y: Int }` was a type error. Fixed by driving `PatRecord`'s sub-patterns from the EXPECTED type — already threaded through `infer_pattern` as an optional `~expected` argument, used before this change only to disambiguate an ambiguous bare constructor name in `PatCon` — instead of synthesizing a type from the pattern alone: when `expected` resolves to a record (via `expand_record`, which accepts a structural `TRecord` or a nominal `TCon` naming one), each mentioned field unifies against the expected type's field, fields the pattern doesn't mention are simply not bound, and the pattern's own type is the expected type unchanged. Naming a field the record doesn't have is now a dedicated `unknown_record_field` diagnostic rather than a unification mismatch. When `expected` doesn't resolve to a record, the ORIGINAL closed-synthesis rule is the fallback (unchanged) — it is the only thing that can constrain an otherwise fully unconstrained scrutinee. Also extended `PatTuple` to thread a per-element expected type to its own sub-patterns (from ITS `expected`, when that resolves to a `TTuple`) — this matters for a record pattern nested inside a tuple pattern whose element types are independently known (e.g. two separately-annotated values matched together, `match (a, b) do (_, { w: w }) -> … end`); confirmed load-bearing by reverting the `PatTuple` change alone and watching that exact case fail again.

**Narrower than the originating task brief assumed, investigated and documented rather than silently over- or under-delivered:** the brief's own motivating example — that this ALSO opens a bare record pattern used directly as a function parameter, e.g. `fn width({ w: w }) : Int do w end` called with a wider `{ w: 8, h: 9 }` — does not typecheck, and cannot with this fix alone. Traced two independent, compounding reasons, both confirmed by direct compilation of the literal example: (1) `desugar_fn_def`'s general path (`lib/desugar/desugar.ml:746`) does not wrap a single (arity-1) parameter into a tuple at all — `scrutinee = EVar arg_name`, `pat = p` directly, no `PatTuple` — so `PatTuple`'s new threading never engages for a one-parameter function regardless of the parameter's pattern shape (only arity ≥ 2 wraps); (2) `fn_param`'s grammar (`parser.mly:413`, `p = pattern { FPPat p }`) gives a bare pattern parameter no type-annotation slot at all — only `name : Type` can carry one — so such a parameter's type has no source but the pattern itself, and is necessarily closed to exactly the fields it names; no amount of `expected`-threading inside `infer_pattern` can open it, because there is nothing to source an `expected` type from. To open a parameter's field list, it must be given a name and an annotation, then destructured via an explicit `match` in the body (`fn f(r : {w:Int,h:Int}) do match r do {w:w} -> w end end`), which routes back through the now-open `PatRecord` rule. Similarly (a separate finding), a `let` binding's own `infer_pattern` call sites never thread `~expected` — the binding IS what establishes the type, so there's nothing upstream to drive from — so `let { x: px } = p` still requires every field of `p`'s type; confirmed by direct compile against both a record literal and a nominal record type. Neither gap is new (both predate this task and are unaffected by it), and neither was in the originating brief's file list or its own TDD tests (scoped to match arms only) — left unchanged, documented rather than silently claimed or silently left inconsistent between the code and the docs.

The compiled golden (`test/native/record_pattern_partial.march`) was written to reflect this: `classify` exercises the match-arm case (two arms mentioning disjoint field subsets, forcing `expand_record_column`'s union-projection), and `width` exercises the `PatTuple`-threading case via two ANNOTATED parameters matched with an explicit `match (dims, scale) do ({ w: w }, s) -> … end` — not a bare `{ w: w }` parameter, for the reason above. Verified both interpreted (`test/test_eval.ml`'s `record_patterns` group gained `test_eval_record_pattern_partial` — this one already passed before the typecheck fix landed, for a legitimate reason: `eval.ml`'s tree-walking interpreter's own `PatRecord` matcher, `eval.ml:1178`, looks fields up by name in the record's full field list and was already open-field-list-tolerant, independent of the typechecker; only the COMPILED path, gated on typecheck, actually exercises this fix) and typechecked (`test/test_compiler.ml`'s `match_diagnostics` group gained `test_partial_record_pattern_typechecks` and `test_record_pattern_unknown_field_rejected` — the latter already reported an error before this change, but for the wrong reason, a field-set mismatch rather than a missing-field diagnostic; confirmed it now fails for the right reason). Docs updated in the same commit: `specs/lang/pattern-matching.md` + `docs/pattern-matching.md` (rewrote "Record Patterns" — open field lists in `match`, the `unknown_record_field` error, and the two positions that remain closed, each with a worked example; also fixed a pre-existing Task 3 doc bug found in passing — `fn area({ w: w, h: h } : { w : Int, h : Int })` is not valid March syntax, confirmed via direct parse failure, since a bare pattern parameter cannot carry a `: Type` annotation); `specs/lang/core-march-types.md` (`(P-Record)` split into "expected known"/"expected unknown" rules, plus a dated note covering both the fix and its two closed-position limitations). `scripts/check-docs.sh` green. ## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, record patterns (`{ x, y: p }`) gained a grammar production and both TIR lowering paths)

**`PatRecord` is reachable from surface syntax, for field lists that exactly match the record's own fields.** Task 3 of `specs/plans/2026-07-24-pattern-matching-gaps.md`. `PatRecord` was fully implemented in the AST, interpreter (`eval.ml:1178`), and typechecker (`typecheck.ml:3544`) from the start, but `lib/parser/parser.mly` had no production that ever built one (confirmed: `grep -c PatRecord lib/parser/parser.mly` returned 0), and — unlike the as-pattern gap Task 2 closed — BOTH TIR lowering paths were unready: `lib/tir/lower_match.ml:205`'s match-matrix compiler failed loudly on `PatRecord`, and `lib/tir/lower.ml`'s `bind_subpat` (the irrefutable-`let` path) had a catch-all that silently returned the body unchanged, which would have left every pattern-bound name resolving as an undefined global fn reference had the grammar landed alone — a silent miscompile, not a loud failure. Fixed with a new `simple_pattern` alternative `LBRACE record_field_pat,* RBRACE` building `PatRecord`, plus `record_field_pat: name COLON pattern | name` (bare `name` puns to `name: name`, mirroring record-literal punning); `token_filter.ml`'s `is_pattern_start` gained `LBRACE`. Adds zero new shift/reduce conflicts (still 9, confirmed with `menhir --explain`). Match-matrix lowering: new `record_fields_in_column`/`expand_record_column` in `lower_match.ml` — a record carries no ctor tag, so instead of dispatching on it, the first record column is expanded into one fresh-variable column per field name (the sorted union of field names across all rows in the column, so every row expands to the same arity), each field projected via `ELet(f_<name>, EField(scrut, name), …)` around the recursive call; this makes a refutable sub-pattern nested inside a record field (`{ code: 404, msg: m }`) dispatch correctly for free, since it lands in an ordinary column once expanded. `let`-binding lowering: new `PatRecord` arm in `lower.ml`'s `bind_subpat`, mirroring the existing `PatTuple` arm — one `ELet` per named field (wildcard fields contribute no binding), recursing through a fresh intermediate variable for compound sub-patterns. Field types matter for both paths: a field var left at `Lower_types.unknown_ty` makes Perceus treat an unboxed scalar as RC-managed, corrupting compiled output for scalar fields (e.g. `Float`); `field_ty` tries the scrutinee's own structural `TRecord` type first, falls back to the typechecker's recorded type for the sub-pattern's own span, and only then gives up with `unknown_ty`. Verified both interpreted (`test/test_eval.ml`'s new `record_patterns` group: match arm, punned fields, `let` binding, function parameter, and a refutable sub-pattern forcing real per-field dispatch) and compiled (`test/native/record_pattern.march`, diffed against `.expected` — match arm, `let`, fn param, and a two-arm `classify` function dispatching on the same field's value). One diagnostics-quality gap noted, out of this task's scope: the typechecker's redundancy/exhaustiveness analysis still treats any top-level `PatRecord` as `SPWild` (`typecheck.ml:3624`) — a safe over-approximation given records are single-constructor and thus irrefutable at the top level, but it means two record-pattern arms discriminating on different literal values of the SAME field produce a false-positive "this pattern can never be reached" warning (confirmed non-fatal: the arm still lowers and runs correctly, output matches `.expected` exactly). The grammar conformance corpus's former reachability witnesses (`reject/r02_record_pattern_in_arm_unreachable.march`, `reject/r07_record_pattern_in_let_unreachable.march`) are retired and replaced by `parse/p30_record_pattern_in_arm.march`/`parse/p31_record_pattern_in_let.march` (both well-typed, `--check` exit 0); corpus is 31 parse + 12 reject = 43 total, `grammar-check` green. Full suite: `run_compiler` 545/545, `run_eval` 247/247, `run_codegen` 444/444, `run_stdlib` 815/816 — the one non-pass is the same pre-existing, machine-wide ASAN 30s livelock in `MARCH_SANITIZE` teardown (verified independent: a trivial unrelated `clang -fsanitize=address` hello-world hangs identically on this host).

Feature list addition:

- Record patterns (`{ x, y: p }`) in `match` arms, `let` bindings, and function parameters — destructures a record's fields, with bare-name punning (`{ x }` for `{ x: x }`). At this point, field lists still had to name every field of the scrutinee record exactly; see the open-field-list entry above for the follow-on.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-25, or-pattern alternatives may bind — the filed follow-up was already half-built)

**The restriction outlived its reason by two commits.** Or-patterns shipped rejecting any alternative that bound a variable, on the stated grounds that the shared arm body is reached through a 0-ary join point with nowhere to put a per-alternative binding, and lifting it was filed as needing n-ary join points. The final-review fix for "an or-pattern arm that binds ANYTHING fails to compile" (`4fdcb527`) had to build exactly that machinery for a different reason — an arm binding OUTSIDE the or, like `P(x, 1 | 2)` — so by the time the follow-up was picked up, `hoist_fallback_jp` already took `?params`, `pat_binder_vars` already collected the arm's binders, `collect_pat_names` already recursed through `PatOr`, and the call site already passed them as arguments. The lowering needed **no change at all**; the only thing left was the typecheck rule. Verified by construction rather than assumption: `A(x) | B(x) -> x * 10` and a two-alternative record form both produce identical output interpreted and compiled.

The rule that replaced the blanket rejection: alternatives must bind the **same names at the same types**. A name only some alternatives supply has no value to pass on the paths that don't (`A(x) | B(y)` — reported as "Or-pattern alternatives must bind the same variables", listing which side each name came from); a name supplied at two types has no single parameter type (`A(x) | B(x)` over `A(Int) | B(String)` — reported against a dedicated reason naming `x`, rather than the misleading "All branches of a match must have the same type" that the generic match-arm reason produced). Corpus: `types/reject/t82` rewritten to pin the disagreement case it now actually tests, and a new `types/accept/t91` pins the agreeing case (173 total, 91 accept + 82 reject). The `or_pattern.march` native golden gained an `unwrap(Left(v) | Right(v))` case, which is the one that exercises argument threading through the join point.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-25, record patterns open in `let`/`let?`; record field-mismatch note polarity fixed)

**`let { code: c } = p` works, and the reason it didn't was smaller than the filed follow-up claimed.** The note carried forward from Task 4 said a `let` binding "is what establishes the type, so there is nothing to drive the pattern from" — true only when the RHS type is genuinely unknown. In `let pat = rhs` the RHS is inferred FIRST (`infer_let_annotated`/`infer_expr`, the line directly above), so an expected type was sitting right there and simply wasn't passed. Threading `~expected` through the five binding call sites — block `ELet`, tail-position `ELet`, top-level `DLet`, and both `let?` sites (where `t_ok` has already been unified with the Ok payload by the time the pattern is inferred) — opens the field list in all of them, exactly as the match path has done since Task 4. The remaining closed position is a bare pattern used directly as a function parameter, which genuinely has no annotation slot to source a type from; that one is unchanged and stays documented. Side benefit: an unknown field in a `let` now produces the dedicated `unknown_record_field` diagnostic ("Available fields: code, msg") instead of `expected \`{ code : u2 }\` but got \`P\``, which leaked an internal type-variable name.

**A record type-mismatch note had its two sides swapped.** `report_mismatch`'s parameters are named against their user-facing meaning — the one called `expected` holds what was PROVIDED, the one called `found` holds what was REQUIRED (documented in the convention comment on the function). The `TRecord`/`TRecord` note read the pair the other way round, so passing `{ w: 8, h: 9 }` where `{ w : Int }` was required reported `` Field `h` is present in the expected type but missing in the found type `` — precisely backwards, `h` being present in what was provided and absent from what was required. The loop also only ever iterated the provided fields, so the reverse case (a field the required type names and the value lacks) produced no note at all. Both directions are now reported, surplus first, naming the two sides in words rather than reusing the overloaded "expected"/"found" pair. Found while checking whether the deferred Minor-8 finding still reproduced; the provenance half of that finding (the "expected type comes from here" span pointing at the argument rather than at the parameter pattern that narrowed it) is untouched and still open — it needs type-provenance threading into `unify`'s diagnostics, a design change rather than a note.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-25, record patterns participate in coverage analysis — `SPRec`)

**The diagnostics carve-out is gone; the cause was removed instead.** `spat`, the exhaustiveness checker's internal pattern shape, had no record case, so `norm_pat` collapsed every `PatRecord` to `SPWild`. That over-claimed coverage in one direction (`match p do { code: 404 } -> ... end` typechecked clean and panicked at runtime on any other `code`) and under-claimed it in the other (the arm *after* a record arm looked unreachable, the false positive `7b90133f` suppressed by excluding record arms from redundancy analysis entirely). Added `SPRec of (string * spat) list` — an assoc list sorted by field name, possibly naming a SUBSET of the record's fields since field lists are open. A record is single-shape, so `find_missing_mc` and `is_useful` treat it exactly as they treat a tuple: specialize into one column per field and recurse. The one difference from `SPTup` is where the arity comes from — the scrutinee's TYPE supplies the full sorted field list, not any single pattern, and `spec_rec_mc` fills a field an arm didn't mention with `SPWild`. That is what lets `{ code: 404 }` and `{ msg: m }` line up in the same matrix column, and it mirrors what `expand_record_column` already does in lowering. With the shape in place the `pat_has_record` carve-out in `check_redundant_arms` was deleted, so a genuinely unreachable record arm is now caught — something the carve-out could never do. Non-enumerable-type handling (`TArrow`/`TChan`/`TLin`/`TNat`) is unchanged; only `TRecord` moved out of that bucket. Missing-case examples render as `{ code: _, msg: _ }`; the `_` for an `Int` field matches what a bare `match n do 404 -> ... end` already prints, so example quality is consistent rather than newly vague. Four regression tests in `match_diagnostics` pin both directions plus the nested-record and stays-silent-when-covered cases. Full suite, `@grammar-check`, `@types-check`, `check-docs.sh`, TIR snapshots, and all four pattern native goldens green; no new non-exhaustive spans appeared in `cap no_panic` stdlib modules (where they would have been promoted to hard errors).

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, record-pattern arms no longer falsely reported unreachable)

**A two-feature interaction bug, caught at the review gate rather than shipped.** With redundancy checking restored on the checking path (entry below) *and* record patterns made reachable (`e360fa1d`), a correct program started emitting a false `redundant_arm` warning: `match p do { code: 404, msg: m } -> m ; { code: c, msg: _ } -> ... end` printed `gone` / `other 200` as expected while warning that the second arm "can never be reached". Cause is `norm_pat`'s `PatRecord -> SPWild` collapse (`lib/typecheck/typecheck.ml:3624`). That direction is safe for **exhaustiveness** — an arm claiming to cover more than it does can only suppress a warning — but is backwards for **redundancy**, where a pattern normalised to "matches everything" subsumes every arm after it. Neither feature alone exposed it: before the checking-path fix the analysis never ran on annotated functions, and before record patterns there was no `PatRecord` to collapse. Fixed by extending `check_redundant_arms`'s existing guarded-arm carve-out (never flagged, excluded from the prefix) to any arm containing a record pattern, via a new `pat_has_record`. Trades some true positives for zero false ones — the right direction for a lint that emits a delete-this-code fix-it. Regression test `record-pattern arm not flagged redundant` in the `match_diagnostics` group. `specs/plans/2026-07-24-pattern-matching-gaps.md`'s "Not in scope" section carried the incorrect "under-reports rather than over-reports" reasoning that missed this; corrected in place.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, redundant-arm warnings restored on the checking-mode typecheck path)

**Unreachable match arms are reported again in the common case.** `lib/typecheck/typecheck.ml` typechecks a `match` on two paths — inference mode (`infer_expr`, ~line 5495) and checking mode (`check_expr`'s `EMatch` arm, ~line 5324). Both called `check_exhaustiveness`; only the inference path also called `check_redundant_arms`. Since a function body with a declared return type is *checked* rather than inferred, every `match` inside a return-annotated function — i.e. most matches in real code — silently skipped unreachable-arm analysis. Demonstrated directly before the fix: `fn f(o : Option(Int)) : Int do match o do _ -> 9 ; Some(x) -> x ; None -> 0 end end` produced no diagnostic, while the identical body with the `: Int` annotation removed produced two `redundant_arm` warnings. One-line fix (add the missing call after `check_exhaustiveness` at the checking-mode site). Two regression tests pin both paths (`match_diagnostics` group, `test/test_compiler.ml`). Notably the restored check surfaced **zero** previously-hidden dead arms anywhere in `test/` or `stdlib/` — the suite's failure set is byte-identical before and after, verified by a revert-to-base control run.

Feature list addition:

- Redundant (unreachable) match-arm warnings on both the inference and checking typecheck paths

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, record field preconditions integrated with String + ADT-tag refinements)

**The record-precondition branch is merged with `main`'s predicate-vocabulary foundation, ADT constructor tags, String refinements, and the two solver-robustness fixes.** The branch had forked before all five and edited the same functions in `lib/refinecheck/refine_check.ml` (7 conflicts), so the integration was resolved on meaning rather than by taking a side. The substantive decisions:

- **`sig_of_clause` collects through `main`'s `refined_param_ty`, not the branch's `refined_scope_ty`.** The branch had widened the Int-only collector to admit records; `main` had independently widened it to admit String and *any registered ADT*. Since a record type IS a registered 1-constructor ADT, `refined_param_ty` already admits records and reports the same `M_Config` sort name the record path keys on — so all four refinable bases (Int, String, variant, record) reach `fn_sig.refined` through one predicate, with no record-specific clause.
- **The call-site dispatch is a three-way `mode`, not a two-way one.** `rparam.sort` is now `Some _` for three different things, so a new `is_record_sort` distinguishes the record case (which installs a `resolve_field` closure) from String (`str_sort`) and from a plain variant (whose tags `main` handles through `resolve_tester`, needing no field selectors). Everything non-record takes `main`'s paths byte-for-byte.
- **The record preamble was dropped in favour of `main`'s.** The branch attached `record_vc_preamble ()` / `type_only_preamble ()` — *all* registered record sorts — whenever the subject was a record. A VC that also mentions an ADT or a measure would then declare the same sort twice, and z3 rejects a duplicate sort inside one push. The record path now simply seeds its sort into `main`'s `adt_sorts`, so it inherits the existing `~skip`/`~skip_elem` deduplication against the measure preamble and the independently-composable `$Str` preamble. Pinned by a test asserting exactly one violation in a module using records, strings, ADTs and Ints together.
- **The two `resolve_measure_app` implementations compose rather than replace.** `main`'s recognises `len` on a declared `Str` constant; the branch's evaluates a measure on a record field selector. A `Str` constant is never a selector, so the string rule is tried first and the record rule handles the remainder — neither changes the other's behaviour.
- **Both solver-poisoning fixes are kept, and both were confirmed to still have an effect.** The branch's field sort-check prevents a malformed VC being built; `main`'s `read_verdict` error-skipping contains one that slips through. Disabling either in turn and re-running the combined fixture showed each is load-bearing: with the sort-check off, the solver reports 2 errored VCs but `main`'s containment keeps every later verdict correct; with it on, zero errored VCs are produced at all.

**Two real defects surfaced during the false-positive sweep, and both were fixed.** The combined-subject fixture — a record, a string, an ADT tester and a plain `takepos(-3)` violation in one module — reported the *correct* `nonempty("hello")` and `unwrap(Some(7))` calls as violations. Root cause was a pair of stacked bugs. (1) The field sort-check was **shallow**: `history: Cons(1, Nil)` places a well-sorted `M_List` constructor at an `M_List` field, but `Cons`'s own head field is declared `Elem` (the built-in `List` is generic, so its element sort is opaque) and the scalar reflection hands it the integer `1`. `(Cons 1 Nil)` reached z3. (2) z3 rejected it with a **multi-line** `(error …)`, and `read_verdict` skipped only the first line — the continuation stayed in the pipe and was consumed as the *next* query's verdict, shifting every later answer by one. That is strictly worse than an unchecked call: under the definite-failure stance a later, unrelated, *correct* call inherits some other VC's `unsat` and is reported. `term_fits_sort` now recurses into a constructor's arguments, and `read_verdict` consumes the whole error s-expression, counting parens only outside its quoted message. Neither bug was reachable from either branch alone — the record call-site path is this branch's, the multi-line error needed a nested sort mismatch to provoke it.

`test/test_refinecheck.ml` stands at **137 tests, all passing on a cold VC cache** (`main` was 124; the branch added 11 record cases, and this integration added 2 more pinning the nested sort mismatch and the four-subject channel-survival shape). All 19 suites are registered in `Alcotest.run`. `test_refine` (22), `run_compiler` (543), `run_eval` (240) and `scripts/check-docs.sh` all exit 0. Adversarial false-positive sweep, cold cache, over ten hand-written programs that are correct at runtime — a satisfying record literal, an unknown record variable, an unknown field value, a forwarded record refinement, a satisfying and an unknown string, `unwrap` inside a `Some(v) ->` arm, and both the ADT and Int path-shadow guards, plus one module using all four subjects together — **all exit 0**, alongside seven positive controls that must and do report.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement types: record field PRECONDITIONS checked at call sites)

**A record refinement is now checked on the parameter side, not just the return side.** Record refinements (`{v : Config | v.port >= 1}`) already discharged as postconditions, but the call-site half checked nothing: `sig_of_clause` collected refined params through `refined_int_ty`, so a record-typed refined parameter never reached `fn_sig.refined` at all, and even had it, `check_call` passed no `resolve_field` closure to `smt_of` — a predicate mentioning `v.port` translated to `None` and the whole predicate was silently dropped. Verified against the compiler before touching anything: on the base commit, a module containing both `fn ret_bad() : {v : Config | v.port >= 1} do { port: 0 } end` and `fn call_bad() : Int do serve({ port: 0 }) end` reported exactly one diagnostic — on `ret_bad`. Both are now reported.

Three wires, no new machinery. (1) `rparam` gained a `sort : string option` and `sig_of_clause` collects through `refined_scope_ty`, so a record param reaches `fn_sig.refined` carrying its SMT sort name. (2) `check_call` reflects a record **actual**: a record literal becomes its constructor applied to the field terms *in declaration order* (record-literal syntax does not require declaration order, so fields are matched by name via `ctor_field_names` — pinned by a control that writes the fields reversed and would go silent under a mis-ordered reflection); a variable holding a record-refined local/param becomes an opaque datatype constant carrying that local's own predicate as an assumption, which is what makes forwarding to a same-shaped parameter work. Anything else — an unrefined record variable, a call, a field access — reflects to `None` and the call is SKIPPED. If *any* field of a literal fails to reflect, the whole record fails: a partial reflection would assert facts about fields the checker cannot see. (3) The VC gets the record `declare-datatypes` preamble under exactly `check_post`'s rule (`record_vc_preamble ()` when an axiomatised measure survived into the goal, `type_only_preamble ()` otherwise), so record and measure sorts coexist in one VC without a duplicate-sort error.

**The record path deliberately does NOT use `check_post`'s report-on-SAT branch.** That branch — reached when `scope_has_record` is true — reports a satisfiable counterexample rather than skipping it, inverting the definite-failure default, and it is the one place in this subsystem where a mistake surfaces as a false positive instead of silence. The call-site record path keeps the same two-discharge procedure as the Int path (report only when the *negated* goal verifies), which turns out to be sufficient: a record literal violating the predicate refutes definitely, and a contradictory forwarded refinement (`v.port <= 0` into `v.port >= 1`) refutes definitely, while a merely *weaker* one (`v.port >= 0`) is neither provable nor refutable and stays silent. `scope_has_record`, `scope_facts`, and `check_post` are untouched by this pass.

**Found and fixed a pre-existing solver-poisoning bug while sweeping for false positives.** The scalar reflection declares every variable it meets as `SInt`. A record field of a non-`Int` type bound to a variable — `{ port: 8080, name: n }` where `name : String` has SMT sort `Elem` — therefore built a constructor application whose argument sorts contradicted its own `declare-datatypes`. Z3 answers such a query with an `(error …)` rather than sat/unsat, and that error desynchronises the long-lived `z3 -in` channel shared by the whole compilation: **every later VC came back inconclusive and reported nothing.** Demonstrated with a module where a `take_n(-3)` two functions after such a record went completely unreported (exit 0), and reported again the moment the record call was removed. The failure mode is silence, so no error-asserting test could have caught it. `reflect_record_literal` now checks each field term against its declared sort from `ctor_field_sorts` and reflects the record only when every field fits — Int/Bool fields take any scalar term that is not a constructor application, a datatype field takes only a constructor of that sort (so `history: Nil` and `history: Cons(1, Nil)` still reflect while `history: xs` does not). The same helper serves `check_post`, so this closes the identical latent hole on the return side, where it predates this pass. Pinned by a paired test: one asserting the record is skipped, one asserting an unrelated `Int` violation *after* it is still reported.

Also moved `make_field_resolver`, `selector_reduce`, `concrete_len`, `concrete_measure_app`, and `reflect_record_literal` above `check_call` so the call site and `check_post` share one definition of each rather than diverging.

`test/test_refinecheck.ml`'s `record-postconditions` suite gained 11 cases (six call-site, the weaker/contradictory forwarding pair, a record-plus-measure combined-preamble case, and the two solver-poisoning cases) — **97 tests, all passing on a cold VC cache** (up from 86; note the plan for this work quoted a 124-test baseline, which did not match the actual 86 on the branch point). Adversarial false-positive sweep over nine hand-written programs that are correct at runtime — a satisfying literal among other positional args, an unknown field value, a record-refined param shadowed by an inner `let`, a record refinement inside `match` arms and under a `when` guard, a function with both a record- and an Int-refined param, a record with a `List` field measured by both `len` and a user `@[measure]`, reversed field order, and a non-Int field bound to a variable — all exit 0, plus two positive controls that must and do report. `run_compiler` (543) and `run_eval` (240) exit 0; a stdlib-using program `--check`s clean and runs. Documentation: `specs/lang/refinement-types.md` gained a "Refining a record over its fields" section and a corrected "`Int` and `Bool` only" limitation bullet; `CHANGELOG.md` gained `[Unreleased]` `### Added` and `### Fixed` entries.
## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, String refinements integrated with ADT constructor-tag refinements)

**The String-refinement branch is merged with the predicate-vocabulary foundation and the ADT constructor-tag feature.** The two lines of work had forked from the same base and edited the same functions in `lib/refinecheck/refine_check.ml` (11 conflicts), so the integration was resolved on meaning rather than by taking a side. The substantive decisions:

- **`rparam` carries one `sort : string option` instead of two parallel flags.** The String branch had added `is_str : bool`; the ADT branch had added `sort : string option`. They are the same question asked twice, so the merged field is the sort — `Some str_sort` for a String, an ADT sort name for a tag refinement, `None` for an `Int` — with a single `rp_is_str` predicate as the only place `str_sort` is compared. `refined_param_ty` correspondingly admits all three base types in one function; the String branch's separate `refined_int_ty` and the ADT branch's dead copy of it are both gone.
- **`smt_of` carries both new resolvers.** `?resolve_tester` (ADT) and `?resolve_str_lit` (String) are independent optional arguments, and both new match arms — the `is_<Ctor>` tester and the `LitString` literal — are present and reachable.
- **`known_predicate_fn` = operators ∪ `len` ∪ registered `@[measure]`s ∪ constructor testers.** `len` was already covered via `is_measure`, so the String feature needed no change there and the ADT tester clause survives intact.
- **Path conditions resolve in the CALLER's namespace *and* see strings.** The ADT branch had (correctly) split `path_resolve_var`/`path_resolve_measure`/`path_resolve_tester` out of the predicate resolvers; the String branch had (correctly) threaded `resolve_str_lit`/`resolve_measure_app` into the path translation. Both survive: the path context now uses the caller-namespace trio *with* the string literal table.
- **One new hazard existed only in the combination, and is fixed.** `path_resolve_var` reflects a caller variable through `reflect_scalar`, which unconditionally declares it `Int`. When that same variable had already been declared into the `$Str` sort by the String pre-reflection, the VC would declare one symbol at two sorts — which z3 answers with an `(error …)` line, and a single such line desynchronises the shared long-lived `z3 -in` channel and **silently disables refinement checking for the rest of the compilation**. `path_resolve_var` now yields `Const name` at the string sort when the name is already in `str_names`, mirroring what `resolve_var`'s caller-scope fallback already did, and the VC-assembly step drops any `Int` declaration for a `$Str`-declared symbol as a second line of defence.
- **The three preambles compose.** A VC now attaches the measure preamble (only when an axiomatised measure was reflected), the per-VC ADT datatype declarations (only when a tester was, deduplicated against the measure preamble's sorts and its `Elem`), and the `$Str`/`$strlen` declarations (only when a string was) — in any combination. The string preamble declares only `$`-prefixed names, which no other preamble can produce, so it composes unconditionally. Verified directly by teeing the solver channel: a VC whose goal is `(not (and (> ($strlen $str0) 0) ((_ is Some) (Some _e1))))` is emitted under one push containing `Elem`, `M_Option` and `$Str` together, z3 answers it normally, **zero `(error` lines across the whole run**, and a violation written *later* in the same file is still reported — the direct proof that the channel did not desynchronise.
- **`wellsorted`/`mentions_str` learned the `Smt.IsCtor` term.** A tester is a Bool over a datatype subject, so it is admitted unless its subject drags in a string constant.

**Verification (all with a cold VC cache — `rm -rf .march/cas/vc` before every run, since refinement verdicts are content-addressed and a warm cache makes a negative-space test prove nothing).** `test_refinecheck` stands at **124 tests, exit 0** — 112 from `main` plus the 12 String cases, with all **19** suites defined in the file registered in `Alcotest.run` (counted both ways: 19 `let …_suite` definitions, 19 distinct suite names in the executed output). `run_compiler` 543, `run_eval` 240, `run_snapshots` 31, `run_codegen -q`, `run_stdlib -q` 780, and `scripts/check-docs.sh` all exit 0. Beyond the suites, six must-fire cases (empty string to `len(_) > 0`; over-long string to `len(_) <= 3`; the list-`len` overload guard `at([1,2], 5)`; `unwrap(x)` in a `None ->` arm; `unwrap(None)`; `takepos(-3)`) each exit 1, and eight must-stay-silent cases — including all four path-shadow guards and a module mixing String and ADT refinements so both preambles attach in one compilation — each exit 0.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement types over `String`)

**`{String | len(_) > 0}` and `{String | _ != ""}` are now checkable contracts.** Both already parsed and typechecked (predicate bodies are transparent to `typecheck.ml`), and both were silently skipped — passing `""` to a non-empty-string parameter compiled clean. `refine_check.ml` now models `String` as an **uninterpreted SMT sort**, `len` as an uninterpreted `$strlen : $Str -> Int` with a single non-negativity axiom, and each distinct string literal in a VC as a declared constant with its length pinned and pairwise distinctness from the other literals asserted. That keeps the whole feature inside the EUF + linear-arithmetic fragment `lib/refine/smt.ml` already renders — structurally the same trick as list `len` — and **deliberately avoids Z3's string theory** (`str.len`, `str.++`, the built-in `String` sort, regex); staying decidable and cheap was the explicit scoping decision, not an accident of effort.

**`len` counts BYTES.** This was checked rather than assumed: the `string_length` builtin is `String.length` in `eval.ml` (OCaml bytes) and an alias for `march_string_byte_length` in `llvm_builtins.ml` — `string_length` and `string_byte_length` map to the *same* C symbol, and the language exposes no codepoint-length primitive at all. So bytes is not a conservative fallback, it is the definition, and `String.length` over the (already unescaped) literal reproduces it exactly.

**`len` overload resolution keys on the DECLARED base type**, never on inference: the refinement's own base type for the binder, and the callee's declared parameter type (new `fn_sig.param_str`) for a cross-argument name. Anything else falls through to the existing list handling untouched. A subject whose type doesn't decide the question is skipped rather than guessed — a wrong resolution would assert a *wrong fact*, which is the one outcome this subsystem must never produce.

**Two encoding hazards found and fixed during the work, both of which had corrupted the whole compilation rather than one query.** The solver is a single long-lived `z3 -in` process whose driver reads exactly one verdict line per `(check-sat)`; `Refine.discharge` retries once on a garbage verdict and then marks z3 **unavailable for the rest of the run**. So any VC z3 answers with an `(error …)` line desynchronises the channel and silently disables refinement checking for every later call site — a global loss of diagnostics from one local mistake. (a) The first draft declared the measure as a bare `len`, which collides with any user or stdlib variable of that name; a VC containing both `(declare-fun len …)` and `(declare-const len Int)` is exactly such an error. All three SMT names now carry a `$` (`$Str`, `$strlen`, `$str0`…), which is legal in an SMT-LIB simple symbol but **cannot** occur in a March identifier, so the collision is impossible by construction. (b) A caller variable reflected as an `Int` could be compared against a string constant (`(= u $str0)`), which z3 rejects on sorts. A new `wellsorted` guard admits a string-mentioning term only where it is genuinely well-sorted — as `$strlen`'s argument, or with both sides of an `=`/`≠` being string constants — dropping ill-sorted *assumptions* (weakening hypotheses can only turn a report into a skip, never the reverse) and skipping the VC outright when the *goal* is ill-sorted. Both are pinned by tests that were verified to fail when the fix is reverted.

**A third bug, caught only because the headline feature was probed rather than trusted.** An early draft wrote a `match` dangling directly inside an `if … then`, which silently swallowed the rest of the `else if` chain. OCaml accepted it, and all six string tests plus the other 86 stayed green — but **all non-string variable resolution had stopped working**, so `iszero(5)` against `{Int | _ == 0}` no longer reported. No existing test covered `_ == 0`; the regression was found by comparing against a base-commit build on a hand-written probe. Pinned by a new case.

**Record-path safety.** `refined_scope_ty`'s `string option` slot previously meant "record sort", and `scope_facts` set its `has_record` flag for any `Some _`. That flag switches `check_post` onto the "a SAT model IS a definite violation" path, which is only justified when the scope pins a *concrete record*; an opaque `$Str` pins nothing, so letting a String entry set it would have been a false-positive engine. String entries now take an explicit separate arm that loads the predicate without touching `has_record`, and carry their own `has_string` flag purely to attach the preamble.

Counterexamples also stopped printing uninterpreted-sort witnesses (`strlit_0 = Str!val!0`), which name an element of a sort z3 knows nothing about and read as internal noise; the useful fact (the length) still comes through as an ordinary `$strlen` entry.

**Verification.** New `string-refinements` group in `test/test_refinecheck.ml` (12 cases: 3 rejections, 3 silence/skip guards, the list-`len` overload-regression guard, 3 regression pins for the bugs above, and the 3 literal-equality/guard-interaction cases). `test_refinecheck` stands at **98 tests, exit 0** (up from 86). `run_compiler` 543, `run_eval` 240, `run_codegen` 444, `run_stdlib -q` — all exit 0. Beyond the suites, a **differential noise sweep** over 125 real programs (`bench/*.march` + `test/native/*.march`, all compiled with the full string-heavy stdlib in scope, cold VC cache) produced output **byte-identical** to a base-commit build — zero new diagnostics and zero lost ones. `scripts/check-docs.sh` passes.

**Known gaps, documented rather than papered over.** An `s == ""` guard establishes **no** length in the else-branch: the sort is opaque and distinctness from the empty literal doesn't imply a length without an injectivity axiom, which is out of scope. No prefix/suffix/contains/concatenation/regex reasoning. String *return* refinements are checked at the definition but do **not** propagate to call sites (`return_refine` stays Int-only, so `reflect_scalar`'s `f$retN` constant cannot be minted at the wrong sort). All three are stated in `specs/lang/refinement-types.md`'s new "String Refinements" section.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, refinement path-fact shadowing + caller/callee namespace split)

**Three false positives in the refinement checker, found by review of the ADT constructor-tag branch, are fixed.** All three had the same root shape: a fact that is *about a name* being read in a scope where that name no longer means what it did.

**(1) Path facts survived rebinding scopes.** `scope_shadow` had long enforced "every binding construct must remove its binders' names before adding any refined ones" for the refined-local *scope*, but nothing did the equivalent for the *path context*, so a `None ->` arm's synthetic `is_None(x)` — or, on the older `Int` path, an `if x < 0` guard — stayed attached to `x` through a `let x = Some(1)` on the next line and flagged the following call. `path_shadow` (`lib/refinecheck/refine_check.ml`) is the companion: it drops any path condition whose expression *mentions* a shadowed name, using a new deliberately over-approximate `expr_mentions` (an occurrence anywhere in the subtree counts, even under a nested binder of the same name — over-approximating discards facts, which under the definite-failure stance can only produce silence). It is applied at all five binding sites in `visit` (the `EBlock` `let` threading, `ELam`, `ELetFn`, `EMatch` arm binders, `ELetQ`) and at the two in `tails`, so the return-position postcondition check gets the same protection. Both the ADT and the pre-existing `Int`/`if`-guard instances are fixed; the `Int` case predates the ADT branch.

**(2) A path condition was resolved in the callee's namespace.** `check_call`'s `resolve_var`/`resolve_tester` map a name by `name = rp.binder → self_actual`, else `actual_of_name name → that parameter's actual`. That is correct for a *predicate*, which is written in the callee's namespace — but path conditions are collected at the call site and are written in the **caller's**. With a *named* binder (`fn unwrap(o : {Option(Int) | is_Some(o)})`), a caller that matched its own variable named `o` and then called `unwrap(y)` had `is_None(o)` silently re-pointed at `y`, and the diagnostic said `(e.g. y = None)` about a `y` the checker knew nothing about. `check_call` now has a second, caller-namespace resolver trio — `path_resolve_var` / `path_resolve_measure` / `path_resolve_tester` — used only for the path context; a caller variable always reflects to `Const name`, which is exactly the term `reflect_scalar`/`reflect_dt` give an `EVar` actual, so when the argument really *is* that variable the two sides still meet on the same SMT symbol and narrowing keeps working. Predicate translation is unchanged.

**(3) `--no-measure-axioms` broke tag checking and lied about it.** `register_builtin_adts` / `register_adt_names` / `register_field_sorts` sat inside `if measure_axioms then begin`, so with the flag off `adt_ctors` was empty, `ctor_of_tester` returned `None`, and the vocabulary warning claimed `` `is_Some` is not a measure or known predicate `` — a false statement about a supported predicate. The three registrations are hoisted out of the guard: constructor-tag refinements build their own small per-VC datatype preamble (`adt_vc_preamble`) and pay none of the quantifier cost the flag exists to avoid, so the flag now affects measures only, as documented.

Also: `is_adt_base`'s `[@@warning "-32"]` is removed (it has had a real caller since the tag feature landed), and the `as`-pattern narrowing limit — sound but previously undocumented — is now listed alongside the other three in `specs/lang/refinement-types.md`. The pre-existing test "narrowing does not leak past a rebinding pattern binder" asserted nothing (both arms were `-> 0`, so no call was ever checked and it passed with or without the guard); it now calls `unwrap` on the rebound name.

`test/test_refinecheck.ml` stands at **112 tests, exit 0** (up from 104): six new rebinding/namespace regressions in `adt-tags`, one `let`-rebinds-a-guarded-`Int` case in `path-sensitivity`, and two `--no-measure-axioms` tag cases in `flag-gating`. Each was confirmed RED before the fix. The narrowing feature still fires on all three of its positive cases (`unwrap(x)` in a `None ->` arm, `unwrap(None)`, `area(Square(2))` — `--check` exits 1 on each). `run_compiler`, `run_eval`, `run_stdlib -q`, `run_codegen -q`, `run_snapshots`, `test_refine` and `scripts/check-docs.sh` all exit 0.

**Known residual (not fixed here):** `check_post` has the same caller/callee conflation in its own `resolve_var` (`name = binder → tail_term`), so a *named* return binder colliding with a local variable could misattribute a path fact. In practice return binders are almost always `_`, which is not a usable expression variable; left as a separate item rather than restructuring `check_post` under this review.

## Current State (as of 2026-07-24, ADT constructor-tag refinements)
